[SYSTEM]
You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L6 adds hepatic-clearance and metabolic-stability experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for systemic presystemic loss while preserving species, assay system, and measurement direction; they are not direct oral- bioavailability results or extra gold votes.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: The closest L1 analog with direct absolute oral bioavailability evidence, imipramine-N-oxide, showed 100% systemic availability after oral dosing versus IV in healthy volunteers, supporting high oral bioavailability in the tricyclic dibenzoazepine series.

L4 records for the close analog oxcarbazepine show essentially complete absorption after a single oral radiolabeled dose in humans (C147), almost complete absorption after oral tablets (C109), and classification as highly permeable in mouse jejunum Ussing-chamber studies (C106).

L3 records after oral carbamazepine dosing show measurable systemic exposure of its metabolite carbamazepine-10,11-epoxide: AUC0-120 120.7 µmol·h/L after a single 200 mg oral dose (C76), Cmax 2.1 µmol/L (C85), and AUC12 9.98 µg·h/mL at steady state (C97), consistent with oral absorption of carbamazepine.

L5 Caco-2 bidirectional data for the tricyclic analog imipramine show Papp A-B 10.8 × 10^-6 cm/s, Papp B-A 12.1 × 10^-6 cm/s, efflux ratio 1.1 (C148, C151, C184), high absorption (C183), and no change in P-gp-mediated efflux with taurocholate (C191), indicating no significant gut-wall efflux in this scaffold.

L6 hepatic evidence for carbamazepine itself is limited but not indicative of extensive first-pass loss: cimetidine increased carbamazepine and its 10,11-epoxide half-life by only 10–20% in humans (C202), and isolated perfused rat liver intrinsic formation clearance of carbamazepine-10,11-epoxide was about 6 ml/min (C226, C239).

evidence_gaps: No direct absolute oral bioavailability (oral vs IV) measurement for carbamazepine is present in the supplied records.
L6 hepatic clearance records for carbamazepine are limited to epoxide formation and half-life modulation; no human intrinsic clearance or hepatic extraction fraction for carbamazepine is supplied.
Most L6 records are for oxcarbazepine/MHD or other tricyclics and are not directly transferable to carbamazepine.
L3 exposure records lack IV comparators, so they inform absorption but do not quantify F.
Some L1/L2 contexts are from cirrhosis or fed conditions and may not match a general healthy adult oral condition.
content.decision_summary: Predicted high: direct L1 analog imipramine-N-oxide had 100% oral systemic availability (C06, C23); L4 oxcarbazepine records show essentially complete absorption and high permeability (C147, C109, C106); L3 oral carbamazepine exposure records show measurable systemic metabolite exposure (C76, C85, C97); L5 imipramine gut-wall data show no significant efflux (C148, C151, C183, C184, C191); L6 hepatic evidence shows only moderate carbamazepine metabolism (C202, C226, C239). No affirmative threshold-relevant evidence supports F < 20%.

You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L6 adds hepatic-clearance and metabolic-stability experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for systemic presystemic loss while preserving species, assay system, and measurement direction; they are not direct oral- bioavailability results or extra gold votes.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.
